Comanche. A Great Plains and Southwest nation historically inhabiting Texas, Oklahoma, Colorado, and Kansas. They were renowned as skilled mounted warriors and master horsemen, organizing themselves into independent bands and leading a mobile, buffalo-hunting culture before fiercely resisting U.S. expansion.

A Shoshonean-speaking people, tradition holds that the Comanche split from the Shoshone and migrated south to the Plains around 1700, acquiring horses and transforming into formidable mounted raiders. They organized themselves into autonomous bands—the Yamparika, Kotsoteka, Quahadi, and Penateka—each led by independent chiefs, with decisions made by consensus in band councils.

The Comanche became legendary for their horsemanship and cavalry tactics, mastering raiding warfare against Spanish, Mexican, and American settlements and rival tribes. One of their greatest leaders was Quanah Parker, half-Comanche and half-American. He led the last band of free Comanche warriors, holding out in the Palo Duro Canyon until surrendering in 1875.

The Comanche hunted buffalo extensively, but the buffalo's near-extinction and confinement to the Comanche Reservation in Indian Territory, now Oklahoma, devastated their traditional economy. Today about fifteen thousand Comanche are enrolled in the Comanche Nation of Oklahoma, and the Comanche language and cultural traditions remain strong among tribal members. They share the Great Plains legacy with neighboring warriors like the Lakota Sioux and Cheyenne.
